title: Expected behavior (preview): B200 hardware profile — early access
author: Noah Patel
content:
h1. Summary

This page describes *expected behavior for the B200 early-access profile* in Redwood Serving Runtime. It is intentionally conservative and should be treated as *provisional* until we complete a full benchmark matrix and fleet standardization.

B200 support is currently:
* *Opt-in only* (not default in Hosted).
* Guarded by *strict compatibility checks* (driver/CUDA/firmware + runtime version).
* Expected to iterate quickly (profile pack versions may change week-to-week during bring-up).

h2. Goals (what “expected behavior” means for B200)

For early-access B200 nodes, a “healthy” system should show:
* Stable latency under mixed workloads (no unexplained p99 spikes due to queueing or kernel fallback).
* Predictable memory headroom (no burst-driven OOMs; bounded fragmentation).
* Deterministic kernel selection (low fallback rate; kernel choice consistent across runs for the same workload bucket).
* Clear observability to support safe rollback (profile_id + profile_version + sku must be visible in runtime metrics and debug endpoints).

h2. Non-goals (early access)

During preview, we are *not* optimizing every model family or context length:
* No guarantee of best-in-class performance for every long-context configuration.
* No guarantee of optimal FP8/quantized paths across all architectures.
* No guarantee of parity with H100 operational maturity (alerts/runbooks will evolve as we learn).

h1. Scope and assumptions

h2. Hardware scope

This doc applies to nodes detected as one of the B200 SKUs in the profile pack compatibility matrix, for example:
* *B200-SXM* (preferred for early access)
* *B200-PCIe* (treated as distinct for tuning; may have different safe defaults)

If the runtime cannot confidently map the node to a supported B200 SKU variant, the B200 profile must *not* be selected.

h2. Runtime + profile pack scope

* Minimum runtime: *runtime-1.22* (or newer) with profile pack support.
* B200 profiles are only supported with an explicit pin to a preview profile version (see “Selection and pinning”).

h2. Workload buckets (used for expected behavior)

We use the same high-level buckets as the scheduler work:

* *Short*: small prompts, short decodes (chat-style)
* *Medium*: moderate prompts and decodes (assistant + tool calls)
* *Long*: long prompts and/or long decodes (docs, RAG with heavy context)

Bucket thresholds are defined in the benchmark matrix doc and encoded in the runtime’s workload classifier. If the classifier is mis-bucketing, most “expected behavior” comparisons will be misleading.

h1. Selection and pinning (B200 is opt-in)

h2. Selection rules (preview)

During preview we require *explicit* pinning for B200:
* If GPU SKU is B200 and *no profile_version is pinned*, runtime will:
  * Select a safe “compatibility only” baseline (if configured), OR
  * Refuse to start (depending on deployment mode policy).

The intent is to prevent silent exposure to unstable defaults while the B200 fleet is still heterogeneous.

h2. Recommended pin

Recommended preview pin for bring-up testing:
* profile_id: *b200_preview*
* profile_version: *1.0.0-b200preview.3* (example; update to the latest vetted build)

Note: The exact version string may change as the pack revs. Always confirm the currently-vetted version in the release note / changelog for the profile pack.

h1. Compatibility notes (must pass to run B200 preview)

h2. Why the compatibility gate is stricter for B200

Early B200 nodes have shown:
* Driver/CUDA mismatches increasing kernel fallback frequency.
* Sensitive interactions between CUDA graphs / kernel variants and certain context-length distributions.
* Greater operational cost of “mystery regressions” due to immaturity of baseline signals.

Therefore, *we prefer a hard fail* over running unknown defaults.

h2. Compatibility requirements (preview)

The runtime enforces an allow-list. At a minimum, bring-up environments must satisfy:

|| Category || Requirement (preview) || Notes ||
| Runtime | runtime-1.22+ | Older runtimes do not expose required profile tags/metrics. |
| NVIDIA driver | >= 570.xx (exact patch per Infra baseline) | Infra owns the baseline; exceptions must be explicitly tracked. |
| CUDA runtime | CUDA 12.4+ (exact minor per baseline) | Mixed CUDA minors across nodes is a top source of noise. |
| MIG | Not supported unless explicitly listed in the profile pack | Default policy: treat MIG as unsupported for B200 preview. |
| Deployment mode | Hosted: canary only; Dedicated: opt-in; Private: supported with explicit pin | See rollout guardrails. |

If any of these fail:
* Hosted/Dedicated: runtime should emit a clear error and fall back to non-B200 capacity (if configured), otherwise fail closed.
* Private: installer should warn loudly; runtime should refuse unsafe config unless operator overrides with an explicit “unsafe_ack” flag (restricted to admin).

h1. Provisional defaults (B200 preview profile)

These are the *starting* defaults designed to be safe under mixed workloads. They will change.

h2. Kernel selection (preview)

* Attention kernel: *blackwell_attn_v1* (preferred) with fallback to *attn_compat_v1*.
* Fallback triggers (expected):
  * Unsupported head dimension / layout for a particular model variant.
  * Context window above the kernel’s validated range.
  * Driver/CUDA combo not in allow-list.

Expected behavior:
* On validated workloads, kernel fallback rate should be *near zero*.
* Any sustained increase in fallback rate generally correlates with increased p95/p99 latency and should be treated as a potential regression.

h2. Scheduler + batching (preview)

We default to a conservative policy biased toward tail-latency stability:

|| Knob || Default (preview) || Rationale / expected effect ||
| scheduler_mode | mixed_workload_v1 | Balances short + long requests to limit starvation. |
| prefill_priority | high | Prevents queue build-up driven by prefill bursts. |
| decode_fairness | enabled | Limits long decode streams from monopolizing the device. |
| max_batch_tokens | conservative (SKU-scaled) | Caps batch growth to protect p99. |
| batch_wait_ms | low | Avoids queueing-induced tail spikes for short bucket. |
| queue_limit | SKU-scaled | Admission control should activate before memory pressure. |

What you should see:
* In short/medium buckets, p99 should be dominated by *compute* more than *queueing*.
* In long bucket, queueing will contribute more, but should still remain bounded and visible.

h2. KV cache + memory headroom (preview)

B200 preview settings reserve additional headroom to reduce OOM/fragmentation risk while we learn real fleet behavior.

|| Knob || Default (preview) || Expected behavior ||
| kv_cache_fraction | conservative (below H100 default) | Lower peak throughput than aggressive settings, but fewer OOMs under burst. |
| allocator_arena_growth | capped | Prevents uncontrolled fragmentation in mixed workloads. |
| compaction_threshold | earlier than H100 | More frequent compaction; watch compaction time counters. |
| admission_control_memory_guard | enabled | Reject/slow requests before crossing headroom boundary. |

Expected behavior:
* Memory usage should plateau below the OOM line with a stable “safety gap” under sustained load.
* Compaction time should be measurable but not dominate end-to-end latency.

h1. Expected performance characteristics (qualitative)

Because B200 is in early access, we frame performance as *directional*.

h2. Prefill vs decode

Typical observations we expect (on validated models and supported drivers):
* *Prefill*: often improves versus H100 at the same batch policy, but is sensitive to kernel selection and driver/CUDA.
* *Decode*: can be comparable to H100 and may be more sensitive to scheduler fairness and cache hit rate.

If you observe:
* Prefill gains but decode regressions: check *scheduler_queue_ms*, *decode_fairness*, and *kv_cache hit/eviction*.
* Both prefill and decode regress: check *kernel fallback rate* and *GPU clocks/utilization stability*.

h2. Tail latency under mixed workloads

In preview, we prioritize predictable tail latency over maximum throughput. Expected behavior:
* p95 should track closely with compute time.
* p99 should not “run away” due to queueing. Large p99 jumps with stable compute time typically indicate scheduler queueing or admission-control misconfiguration.

h1. Bring-up: metrics that must be watched (required)

This section is the *minimum* instrumentation required to operate B200 preview safely. If any of these are missing, do not expand beyond a tiny canary.

h2. Required labels/tags (to avoid blind spots)

All runtime metrics and traces used for validation must be tagged with:
* sku (e.g., B200-SXM)
* profile_id
* profile_version
* workload_bucket
* model_family (coarse; avoid high cardinality)

h2. Required metrics (and what “good” looks like)

|| Metric || Why it matters || Expected / watchouts ||
| request_latency_ms (p50/p95/p99) | Primary SLO signal | Regression if p99 increases without explained workload shift. |
| scheduler_queue_ms (p50/p95/p99) | Distinguishes queueing vs compute | *Must* stay bounded; rising queue_ms with flat compute indicates scheduler policy issue. |
| stage_latency_ms (prefill/decode) | Separates prefill vs decode changes | Use to detect kernel changes vs KV/cache effects. |
| kernel_fallback_rate | Early warning for driver/CUDA mismatch or unsupported shapes | Any sustained non-trivial fallback rate during validated workloads is suspicious. |
| kernel_choice (counter by variant) | Confirms deterministic selection | Sudden shifts often map to fleet drift or a config change. |
| gpu_utilization, sm_efficiency | Detects underfill vs saturation | Low util + high queueing => scheduler limits too strict or batch policy too conservative. |
| hbm_used_bytes / hbm_free_bytes | Headroom validation | Headroom should remain stable; sawtooth patterns can indicate fragmentation. |
| oom_events / cuda_oom_count | Hard safety gate | Any OOM during canary is a stop signal until explained. |
| kv_cache_hit_rate + eviction_rate | Explains decode throughput/latency | Drops in hit rate often produce decode regressions. |
| kv_compaction_ms + compaction_count | Measures cost of compaction | Spikes can explain tail events; sustained high compaction suggests fragmentation risk. |
| fragmentation_estimate (gauge) | Predicts impending instability | Trending upward over hours indicates allocator tuning needed. |
| error_rate (5xx), timeout_rate | Safety gate | Must remain within rollout guardrails; timeouts often correlate with queueing. |

h2. Dashboards (bring-up checklist)

At minimum, validate using:
* Runtime Profiles overview (adoption, latency by profile_version)
* Kernel fallback panel (rate + kernel_choice distribution)
* Queueing vs compute breakdown (scheduler_queue_ms vs stage_latency_ms)
* Memory health (HBM usage, OOMs, fragmentation, compaction time)

See: Runtime Profile Observability Dashboard Spec.

h1. Bring-up procedure (recommended)

h2. Phase 0 — node sanity

1. Verify SKU detection returns the expected B200 variant.
2. Verify driver/CUDA match the Infra baseline.
3. Start runtime with pinned profile_version and confirm /health includes:
   * sku
   * profile_id
   * profile_version
4. Run a single-model smoke load (short bucket) and confirm:
   * kernel_fallback_rate ~ 0
   * no OOMs
   * queue_ms remains low

h2. Phase 1 — minimal matrix

Run a minimal benchmark subset:
* Short bucket at low concurrency
* Medium bucket at moderate concurrency
* One long bucket scenario (explicitly flagged as higher risk)

Stop conditions:
* Any OOM
* Sustained kernel fallback rate increase
* p99 increase beyond SRE guardrail thresholds without explanation

h2. Phase 2 — mixed workload canary

Run mixed bucket traffic in a canary cohort:
* Concurrency representative of production
* Realistic prompt length distribution
* Include one “spiky” burst test

Only expand cohort size if *both* are true:
* latency deltas are stable over time
* memory + fallback metrics remain within expected ranges

h1. Known failure modes (preview)

h2. 1) Driver/CUDA mismatch → kernel fallback spike

Symptoms:
* kernel_fallback_rate increases
* kernel_choice shifts from preferred kernel to compat kernel
* p95/p99 latency increases, often most visible in prefill

Actions:
* Confirm driver/CUDA versions on the node.
* Compare against allow-list in the pinned profile pack version.
* If mismatch cannot be resolved quickly: rollback to a non-B200 pool / disable B200 canary.

h2. 2) Long-context instability (validated range exceeded)

Symptoms:
* kernel fallbacks for long bucket only
* queueing increases due to reduced throughput

Actions:
* Confirm context windows are within validated range for the preview kernel.
* Temporarily clamp workload bucket routing (route long-context to H100) until kernel validation expands.

h2. 3) Fragmentation/compaction thrash under burst

Symptoms:
* fragmentation_estimate trends upward
* kv_compaction_ms spikes
* intermittent p99 tail events without high GPU util

Actions:
* Reduce max concurrency / tighten admission control.
* Increase memory headroom (reduce kv_cache_fraction).
* Capture allocator debug bundle and file follow-up under the profiles pack epic.

h1. Rollback guidance (must be easy)

Rollbacks should be *profile-first*, not code-first:
* Primary rollback: pin to previous known-good profile_version.
* Secondary rollback: disable B200 canary / route B200 traffic to other SKUs.
* Emergency rollback: kill-switch to disable profile pack selection and use legacy defaults (only if previously validated).

All rollbacks must preserve auditability:
* Record who changed the profile pin, when, and what cohort it affected.

For any B200 canary incident, page Runtime on-call and include:
* profile_id + profile_version
* sku variant
* driver/CUDA versions
* kernel_fallback_rate graph + kernel_choice breakdown
* scheduler_queue_ms and stage latency breakdown

h1. Open items / TODO (tracked)

* Finalize B200 baseline driver/CUDA allow-list with Infra and encode into profile pack.
* Expand benchmark matrix coverage for long-context and mixed quantization settings.
* Define “expected” kernel_fallback_rate thresholds for validated workloads (target: near zero) and add alerting.
* Validate whether B200-PCIe requires distinct admission-control and batching caps.
* Update this page from “preview” to “v1” once:
  * benchmark acceptance thresholds are in place, and
  * fleet heterogeneity is reduced or fully represented in the compatibility matrix.
